implementation_notes: Kotlin's data classes are the memento: the compiler derives equals/hashCode/toString and a copy() function from the primary-constructor properties, so the snapshot is a data-class value - make the properties val and the collections immutable (List/Map/Set or persistent collections) and the value is safe to store. copy() is shallow, and it only covers primary-constructor properties, so mutable components or class-body properties make a 'snapshot' that shares state or silently omits fields. The caretaker is an ArrayDeque<State> (kotlin.collections.ArrayDeque) with an explicit size bound, undo is an assignment, and no nested-class privacy trick is needed because a private state type plus internal constructors already limits who can forge snapshots.
pitfalls: copy() is a shallow copy: a MutableList component is shared between the original and the snapshot, so edits through either side appear in both - use val plus immutable collections, or copy the component explicitly.

The compiler derives copy(), equals() and toString() only from primary-constructor properties: state kept in the class body is silently absent from snapshots and equality, so it must be captured another way.
A data class with var properties can be mutated after being stored as a memento, which breaks the immutability the pattern relies on; prefer val and build successor states with copy().
An unbounded ArrayDeque keeps every state alive, and each retained snapshot holds its whole component graph; bound the history.

variants.name: kotlinx.serialization snapshots for persisted history
variants.implementation_notes: When the undo history must survive the process or travel between components, annotate the state with @Serializable and let the compiler plugin generate the serializer: Json.encodeToString writes the memento to a string or bytes and decodeFromString reconstructs it, so the caretaker can keep snapshots in a file, a database or a message. @Transient excludes derived fields that the originator rebuilds on restore, and the format is explicit, so history stays readable and migratable - unlike Java serialization it does not depend on class binary layout. Use this variant for durable history and the plain data-class copy for hot in-memory undo.
variants.code_sketch:
@Serializable
data class DocState(val text: String, val caret: Int)

val mementos = mutableListOf<String>()          // caretaker keeps JSON
fun save(s: DocState) = mementos.add(Json.encodeToString(s))
fun latest(): DocState = Json.decodeFromString(mementos.removeLast())
pitfalls: Serializers are generated at compile time: every type reachable from the snapshot must be @Serializable, and polymorphic state needs registered subclasses or it fails at runtime.
@Transient members are not restored, so anything excluded must be reconstructible by the originator.
Encoding every snapshot as text inflates memory and CPU compared with holding values; serialize at checkpoints rather than on every change.
